title: The AP U.S. History exam's shape
statement: From May 2027 the Advanced Placement United States History exam has source-based multiple-choice sets, sourced short answers, a document-based essay question and a broad long essay.
example: Multiple choice gives 55 questions in 55 minutes for 40 percent of the score.
detail: An AP history course's design documents summarise the official Course and Exam Description effective Fall 2026, and the figures match pages 497 to 500 of that description and its clarification notice, both read in this run. Multiple choice has 55 questions in 55 minutes for 40 percent, typically in sets of three to four on shared stimuli, each with four options and one defensible key; three required short answers take 40 minutes for 20 percent, the first on secondary text sources, the second on a primary text source and the third on a primary or secondary non-text source, each on a different period and in three one-point parts. The document-based question takes 60 minutes, including a 15-minute reading period, for 25 percent, uses seven documents on developments between 1754 and 1980, and must give students a genuine opportunity to use at least four documents, add outside evidence and explain the situation, audience, purpose or point of view of at least two. The long essay takes 40 minutes for 15 percent and gives one broad prompt over roughly half the course, within which the student chooses the developments; the course scores the document-based question on the current seven-point rubric and the long essay on the current six-point one, and it rejects the source-free short answers its legacy generator allowed.
against: A single unit can only rehearse these forms: one unit's three sourced short answers cannot show the official spread across periods (BRAINLIFT.md lines 285-286), and its three-source task is labelled a mini-DBQ rehearsal (lines 611-612).

evidence.quote: Multiple choice contains 55 questions in 55 minutes and contributes 40 percent. Questions generally sit in source-based sets of three or four.
Four options, one defensible key; standalone use is not a section simulation
55 stimulus-based multiple-choice questions in sets, 40 percent of the exam;
Three required short-answer questions take 40 minutes and contribute 20 percent.

Under the new contract, every SAQ is sourced: question 1 uses one or more secondary text sources, question 2 uses a primary text source, and question 3 uses a primary or secondary non-text source. The three questions focus on different historical periods.
A complete SAQ has three independently achievable one-point parts.
records the all-sourced SAQ sequence and required broad LEQ design for May 2027.
The document-based question contributes 25 percent and allows 60 minutes, including the recommended reading period. It uses seven documents and covers 1754-1980.
one seven-document DBQ covering developments from 1754 to 1980;
The full DBQ uses seven verified documents and the current seven-point rubric:

Students need a genuine opportunity to use at least four documents in an argument, add relevant outside evidence, and explain how the situation, audience, purpose, or point of view of at least two documents matters to their argument.
The long essay contributes 15 percent and allows 40 minutes. It uses one broad prompt, with the student choosing the relevant development or developments within the prompt's scope.
The full LEQ uses a broad prompt and the current six-point rubric:
an official LEQ prompt spans a broad period covering roughly half the course.
The legacy local generator allowed source-free SAQs, so the course rejects that behavior.
Unit 1's three sourced SAQs demonstrate the three source modalities, but the unit cannot demonstrate the official cross-period distribution by itself.
Unit 1 teaches document functions with three sources but labels the task as a Period 1 mini-DBQ rehearsal.
